micronarrative: The scenario’s framing feels lopsided to me. In my experience, locals who attend city council meetings rarely hold protests; those who do are often the ones shouting, waving signs, and disrupting sidewalks. I don’t see the “local” label as fixed—it shifts depending on who shows up and how. When people speak calmly in meetings, presenting facts without yelling, I listen. But loud protests feel performative, even if the message isn’t. I’ve noticed online how voices gain traction based on followers or platforms, not just merit.  The tension isn’t just about migrants or borders. It’s about law and order and the health and safety of the local citizens not the illegals that the gov't bussed in and used our money to house and support illegals who are not local citizens.
